answer: The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.2% (seasonally adjusted) for September 2026, up from 4.1% in August. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Situation report, released October 2, 2026, as carried on FRED (series UNRATE).

About 3.4% year over year for August 2026, the latest month published (September's CPI was not yet out as of October 10, 2026). I calculated this myself from the BLS seasonally adjusted CPI-U index: 334.131 in August 2026 versus 323.291 in August 2025, a rise of 3.35%. Note that the headline 12-month figure BLS quotes in its press release uses the not-seasonally-adjusted index, which I did not check and which can differ by a tenth. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics data via FRED (series CPIAUCSL, updated September 11, 2026).

Total nonfarm payrolls rose by 29,000 in September 2026 (seasonally adjusted), which BLS described as 'changed little'. The level went from 159,015 thousand in August to 159,044 thousand in September. The same report revised July down to -10,000 and August down to +133,000. Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Situation report, released October 2, 2026 (also FRED series PAYEMS).

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.40% for the week ending October 8, 2026, up from 7.28% the week before. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, as published on FRED (series MORTGAGE30US).

The 10-year Treasury yield (constant maturity) was 5.22% on October 8, 2026, the most recent day published when I checked; the October 9 figure was not yet posted. It was 5.28% on October 7. Source: Federal Reserve Board H.15 release, as published on FRED (series DGS10, updated October 9, 2026).

The effective federal funds rate averaged 3.75% for September 2026, up from 3.63% in each of May through August. Source: Federal Reserve Board H.15 release, as published on FRED (monthly series FEDFUNDS, updated October 1, 2026).

Real GDP grew at a 2.2% seasonally adjusted annual rate in the second quarter of 2026 (April-June), after 2.5% in the first quarter. This is the figure as of the September 30, 2026 update. Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, as published on FRED (series A191RL1Q225SBEA).

Housing starts were 1,275,000 at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in August 2026, down from 1,309,000 in July. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and HUD New Residential Construction release, as published on FRED (series HOUST, updated September 17, 2026).

Initial jobless claims were 197,000 (seasonally adjusted) for the week ending October 3, 2026, down from 199,000 the prior week. Source: U.S. Department of Labor Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims report, as published on FRED (series ICSA, updated October 8, 2026).

The latest reading is 46.3 for October 2026, which is a preliminary figure; the final October number is due October 23, 2026. The September 2026 reading was 48.1. Note that FRED lags the survey's own site: its latest value is 51.7 for August 2026. Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

The U.S. unemployment rate in April 2020 was 14.8% (seasonally adjusted, civilian unemployment rate, as currently published). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, read from the FRED series UNRATE. The BLS first reported 14.7% in May 2020; later revisions put it at 14.8%.

The U.S. unemployment rate in October 2009 was 10.0% (seasonally adjusted, as currently published). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, read from the FRED series UNRATE. The first release showed 10.2%, which is from my recollection and not checked in this session.

The highest weekly 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 1981 was 18.63% (U.S. average), in the week dated October 9, 1981. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, read from the FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

The 10-year Treasury yield on March 9, 2020 was 0.54% (market yield at 10-year constant maturity, daily). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15), read from the FRED series DGS10.

Year-over-year headline CPI inflation in June 2022 was about 9.0% on the seasonally adjusted all-urban-consumers index. That is my calculation from the index levels: 294.957 in June 2022 against 270.654 in June 2021 (1982-84=100), a rise of 8.98%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, read from the FRED series CPIAUCSL, current seasonal factors. The widely quoted 9.1% is the not-seasonally-adjusted figure; I did not look that one up in this session.

Housing starts in January 2006 were 2,273 thousand, or about 2.27 million units, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (total new privately owned units started). Source: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, read from the FRED series HOUST.

The lowest monthly University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading in 2022 was 50.0 (index, 1966:Q1=100), in June 2022. Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, read from the FRED series UMCSENT.

The WTI crude oil spot price (Cushing, Oklahoma) on April 20, 2020 was -$36.98 per barrel. The price was negative that day. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, read from the FRED series DCOILWTICO.

The U.S. personal saving rate in April 2020 was 31.8% of disposable personal income (monthly, seasonally adjusted annual rate, as currently published). Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, read from the FRED series PSAVERT. This figure has been revised several times; the first estimate was about 33%, which is from my recollection and not checked in this session.

U.S. real GDP fell at an annualized rate of 28.0% in the second quarter of 2020 (percent change from the preceding quarter, seasonally adjusted annual rate, as currently published). Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, read from the FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA. Earlier estimates differed: from my recollection, not checked in this session, the advance estimate was -32.9% and the third estimate was -31.4%.

The effective federal funds rate averaged 19.04 percent in July 1981 (monthly average, not seasonally adjusted). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15), read from FRED series FEDFUNDS.

The median sales price of houses sold in the U.S. was $442,600 in Q4 2022 (quarterly, not seasonally adjusted), as currently published. This is a revised figure; earlier vintages showed a higher value for that quarter (about $479,500, from memory, not re-checked). Source: U.S. Census Bureau / HUD, read from FRED series MSPUS.

The U.S. unemployment rate averaged about 3.7 percent over the 12 months of 2019 (3.675 percent, the simple mean of the seasonally adjusted monthly rates: 4.0, 3.8, 3.8, 3.7, 3.6, 3.6, 3.7, 3.6, 3.5, 3.6, 3.6, 3.6). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, read from FRED series UNRATE; the average is my calculation.

5 months of 2023: January through May. Year-over-year changes in the seasonally adjusted CPI-U were about 6.3% (Jan), 6.0% (Feb), 4.9% (Mar), 5.0% (Apr) and 4.1% (May). From June to December they were between 3.1% and 3.7%, below 4%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, index levels read from FRED series CPIAUCSL; the year-over-year percentages are my calculation.

The highest weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 2023 was 7.79 percent, for the week of October 26, 2023 (Freddie Mac survey dated Thursday, 2023-10-26). Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, read from FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

About 1.459 million jobs. Total nonfarm payroll employment (seasonally adjusted) rose from 156,857 thousand in December 2023 to 158,316 thousand in December 2024, a gain of 1,459 thousand, on the data as currently published (read 2026-10-10). Benchmark revisions have lowered this well below the roughly 2.0 to 2.2 million reported earlier (earlier figures from memory, not re-checked). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Current Employment Statistics), read from FRED series PAYEMS; the difference is my calculation.

About 129.6 percent. The S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (not seasonally adjusted, Jan 2000 = 100) rose from 134.157 in January 2012 to 308.055 in June 2022. Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, read from FRED series CSUSHPINSA; the percent change is my calculation.

The most negative daily 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread in 2023 was -1.08 percentage points, on July 3, 2023. The next lowest was -1.07 on March 8, 2023. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, calculated from Treasury constant maturity yields, read from FRED series T10Y2Y.

3 quarters, on currently published data: 2020 Q1 (-5.2%), 2020 Q2 (-28.0%) and 2022 Q1 (-1.0%), all seasonally adjusted annualized rates. 2022 Q2 was reported as negative in earlier vintages (from memory, not re-checked) but now shows +0.6%, so it does not count on current data. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, read from FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA.

Seasonally adjusted initial jobless claims peaked at 6,137,000 for the week ending April 4, 2020, on currently published (revised) data. The week ending March 28, 2020 was next at 5,946,000. Original releases at the time showed a higher peak, in the week ending March 28 (about 6.87 million, from memory, not re-checked), before seasonal factors were revised. Source: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, read from FRED series ICSA.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, April 4, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 228,000 in March 2025, seasonally adjusted (159,398 thousand vs 159,170 thousand for February in that vintage). The data now (FRED series PAYEMS, read October 10, 2026, with data through September 2026) show a gain of 67,000 (158,377 thousand in March vs 158,310 thousand in February 2025). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed); the changes are my subtraction of the published levels.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, June 6, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 139,000 in May 2025, seasonally adjusted (159,561 thousand vs 159,422 thousand for April in that vintage). The data now (FRED series PAYEMS, read October 10, 2026) show a gain of 13,000 (158,498 thousand in May vs 158,485 thousand in April 2025). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed); the changes are my subtraction of the published levels.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, July 3, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 147,000 in June 2025, seasonally adjusted (159,724 thousand vs 159,577 thousand for May in that vintage). The data now (FRED series PAYEMS, read October 10, 2026) show a loss of 20,000 jobs (158,478 thousand in June vs 158,498 thousand in May 2025). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed); the changes are my subtraction of the published levels.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, August 1, 2025): total nonfarm payrolls rose by 73,000 in July 2025, seasonally adjusted (159,539 thousand vs 159,466 thousand for June in that vintage). The data now (FRED series PAYEMS, read October 10, 2026) show a gain of 64,000 (158,542 thousand in July vs 158,478 thousand in June 2025). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed); the changes are my subtraction of the published levels.

The advance estimate (BEA, April 28, 2022) put real GDP growth in Q1 2022 at -1.4% (seasonally adjusted annual rate, change from the prior quarter). The current data (FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA, read October 10, 2026) show -1.0%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed).

The advance estimate (BEA, July 28, 2022) put real GDP growth in Q2 2022 at -0.9% (seasonally adjusted annual rate, change from the prior quarter). The current data (FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA, read October 10, 2026) show +0.6%, so the originally reported decline is now a small increase. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed).

The advance estimate (BEA, January 30, 2025) put real GDP growth in Q4 2024 at 2.3% (seasonally adjusted annual rate, change from the prior quarter). The current data (FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA, read October 10, 2026) show 2.4%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed).

4.0%, for January 2025 (seasonally adjusted, U-3). That was the latest month available as of March 1, 2025; the February 2025 figure had not yet been published. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via the ALFRED March 1, 2025 vintage of series UNRATE (St. Louis Fed).

159,536 thousand (about 159.5 million) jobs, seasonally adjusted, for December 2024. That is the figure as it stood on February 1, 2025, before the annual benchmark revision published later that month. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via the ALFRED February 1, 2025 vintage of series PAYEMS (St. Louis Fed). For comparison, the same month is now shown as 158,316 thousand.

About 2.9% both then and now. As first reported (BLS, January 15, 2025), the seasonally adjusted CPI-U all-items index was 317.685 for December 2024 against 308.742 for December 2023, a 12-month rise of 2.90%. The current data (FRED series CPIAUCSL, read October 10, 2026) show 317.604 against 308.741, a rise of 2.87%, which still rounds to 2.9%. The percentages are my calculation from the published index levels (1982-84=100). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED/ALFRED (St. Louis Fed).

The original source is Freddie Mac, from its Primary Mortgage Market Survey. FRED's 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (MORTGAGE30US) is published weekly (week ending Thursday), in percent, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED's copy (SP500, daily close, index, not seasonally adjusted) holds only 10 years of daily history, per the note on the series page. As of October 2026 that means it goes back to roughly October 2016; I did not confirm the exact first observation date.
The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED lists the series (CSUSHPINSA, monthly, index Jan 2000=100) under the release 'S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices'.
It comes from the University of Michigan, from its Surveys of Consumers. The FRED series is UMCSENT: monthly, index 1966:Q1=100, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), from its Spot Prices release. The FRED series is DCOILWTICO (Crude Oil Prices: West Texas Intermediate, Cushing, Oklahoma): daily, dollars per barrel, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration (part of the Department of Labor), from its Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims Report. Yes, the headline series (ICSA) is seasonally adjusted. It is a weekly count of claims, for weeks ending Saturday.
Real GDP on FRED (GDPC1) is reported in billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate. It is quarterly and the source is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

It is an index with base period 1982-1984=100. The headline FRED series (CPIAUCSL, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average) is monthly and seasonally adjusted. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

It is published jointly by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, in the New Residential Sales release. The FRED series is MSPUS: quarterly, in dollars, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, from its H.15 Selected Interest Rates release. The daily FRED series is DFF: percent, 7-day daily frequency, not seasonally adjusted.
